title: HDRTransDC High Dynamic Range Image Reconstruction with Transformer Deformation Convolution

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states the dynamic weight is produced by 'the spatial attention mechanism' and that 'Δw adaptively selects the information of different frames... in different areas,' implying the weight varies by spatial location (consistent with the abstract's claim that DWFB 'spatially adaptively selects useful information'). However, immediately afterward the text says 'we use the weight Δw that is shared in spatial dimension and fully connected in channel dimension,' which describes a channel-wise (not spatially-varying) weighting scheme. This directly contradicts the preceding claim that Δw varies across different spatial areas, and also contradicts the paper's central contribution claim that DWFB performs spatially adaptive fusion.

The seminal Debevec and Malik paper, 'Recovering High Dynamic Range Radiance Maps from Photographs,' was published at SIGGRAPH in 1997, not 2008. Citing it as a 2008 work misattributes the publication date of this foundational HDR reference.

The text states 'the CNN-based method can only extract local features (red points)' and later states 'our TDCAM can extract long-range content (red points) in the non-reference image,' using the identical color label ('red points') to describe the sampled features of two different methods (CNN-based vs. TDCAM) being contrasted in the same figure. This makes it impossible to visually distinguish which points belong to which method as described, indicating an inconsistency between the figure's legend/content and the explanatory text.

The paper states training is performed for '6000 epochs with a batch size of 2' on a dataset of only 74 training scenes. This is an unusually large number of epochs combined with an unusually small batch size, which is atypical relative to comparable HDR deghosting papers (which typically train for a much smaller number of epochs or specify fixed iteration counts), raising concern about the plausibility/correctness of the reported training configuration.
